{"id": "55:6/q01", "question": "What does al-najm refer to here?", "turns_on": "Whether the tree pairing privileges a ground plant, the preceding sun and moon suggest stars, or the shared word is intentionally inclusive; inward readers assign the terms to faculties.", "positions": [{"id": "55:6/q01/p1", "position": "Stemless or low-growing earthly vegetation.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ names grass and herbage; Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAbbās and others distinguish plants without a stem from trunked trees. Al-Suddī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya derive the name from emerging from earth; Ibn al-Aʿrābī notes najma is a small plant and najama describes a horn, star or tooth appearing. Abū ʿUbayda cites al-Ḥārith b. Ẓālim's donkey pulling a plant; al-Azharī explains its strained body; al-Layth and Zuhayr supply plant imagery. Ṣafwān b. Asad's line uses anjama for plants emerging, though al-Wāḥidī says he found no linguist using anjama for growing. Al-Qurṭubī derives najm from appearance. Some define the plant as winter-perishing, al-Muntaqā as growth ending within a year; Bursawī includes vine and pumpkin, Kuran Yolu grain and grass. Ibn Jarīr prefers this sense according to Ibn Kathīr; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and al-Ālūsī favor it for its pairing with shajar. Abū Ḥayyān calls it the apparent reading. Islahi calls the proposed small plants, thorny trees or creepers far-fetched."}, {"id": "55:6/q01/p2", "position": "The heavenly stars, taken collectively.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan and others give this sense; Ibn ʿĀshūr and the Study Quran explain singular najm as collective, while Ibn ʿĀshūr also allows a singular with plural nujūm, citing 53:1 and 52:49. Al-Zajjāj invokes 22:18's celestial prostration; Abū Isḥāq invokes 16:12; Muḥammad b. Yazīd cites poetry for celestial najm. Ibn Kathīr prefers it on 22:18, and Islahi regards it as the conventional sense. Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Ṭabarī choosing the star reading with its moving shadow. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says stars appear in their heavenly realm as trees do on earth."}, {"id": "55:6/q01/p3", "position": "Both earthly vegetation and celestial stars fall within the word.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj derives the breadth from najama, to appear or rise. Al-Biqāʿī includes both sorts of stars and their appointed courses and benefits. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the shared word bridges heavenly and earthly pairs; Qushayrī sets out both referents."}, {"id": "55:6/q01/p4", "position": "Inwardly, it is the sentient animal soul.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī places that soul in the body's night; with the nourishing vegetative soul as tree it turns toward the body's earth to nurture and perfect it."}, {"id": "55:6/q01/p5", "position": "Inwardly, it is the intellect.", "reasons": "Bursawī says intellect guides knowledge but fades before divine realities without unveiling; thought, its tree counterpart, remains confined to natural, imaginative and bodily powers. Both are bounded creatures unable to comprehend the eternal Creator; he cites 39:67."}, {"id": "55:6/q01/p6", "position": "Inwardly, it is the lower powers.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the counterpart tree as higher predispositions; both humble themselves on returning to God."}]}
{"id": "55:6/q02", "question": "What does al-shajar refer to here?", "turns_on": "Whether shajar names its botanical referent or an inward counterpart to najm.", "positions": [{"id": "55:6/q02/p1", "position": "Plants or trees with a lasting stem or trunk.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās and many others oppose this to stemless najm; al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī say its stem endures winter. Al-Muntaqā instead contrasts growth that continues beyond its year with a plant whose growth ends. Ibn ʿAṭiyya relates shajar to interwoven branches. Ibn al-Jawzī calls shajar plural of shajara and notes shajir for a tree-filled valley or land and shajara for human dispute. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies rooted growth with an elevated stem beneficial to people and animals."}, {"id": "55:6/q02/p2", "position": "Inwardly, it is the nourishing vegetative soul.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says it turns to the body's earth with the animal soul to nourish and perfect the body."}, {"id": "55:6/q02/p3", "position": "Inwardly, it is thought.", "reasons": "Bursawī confines it to natural, imaginative and bodily powers; reason and thought circle the created world but cannot encompass God, citing 39:67."}, {"id": "55:6/q02/p4", "position": "Inwardly, it is the higher predispositions.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports their humbling themselves before God on their return to Him."}]}
{"id": "55:6/q03", "question": "How do the star and tree prostrate?", "turns_on": "The notes variously explain sujūd as submission, observable motion or shadow, a literal unseen act, an evidentiary sign, or inward humbling.", "positions": [{"id": "55:6/q03/p1", "position": "They submit to God's will and appointed functions.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba describes inanimate compliance under subjugation; al-Naḥḥās calls submission the broad sense of sujūd, extending to animals and prayer. Ibn al-Jawzī says Arabic sujūd involves lowering the head without necessarily touching the ground and can denote any submission. Al-Jubbāʾī says divine direction meets no resistance. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Bursawī and al-Ālūsī compare natural obedience to willing worship; al-Ālūsī calls it an explicit derivative metaphor. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī specifies obedience in growth and, more precisely, roots penetrating soil for nourishment as dependence. Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits Mujāhid's figurative submission, illustrated by a line about hills prostrating to hooves. Qushayrī says created things' submission precludes their worship."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p2", "position": "They prostrate through shadows that move and turn.", "reasons": "Abū Razīn and Saʿīd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zajjāj and others identify the shadow; al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī cite 16:48, as do al-Baghawī and Bursawī. Al-Farrāʾ makes the bodies face the rising sun and incline with it until the shadow recedes; al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī transmit that detail. Ibn ʿAṭiyya applies vegetation's shadow and turning to either meaning of najm. Al-Qurṭubī reports Mujāhid's moving shadow for the star and al-Ṭabarī's choice. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds their approaching earthly shadows and cites 13:15. Al-Ṭabrisī says shadows reveal a directing Creator."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p3", "position": "The star prostrates by rising.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports Mujāhid and Qatāda; al-Baghawī reports Mujāhid."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p4", "position": "The star prostrates by setting, while the tree makes fruit available.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this alternative, repeated by al-Qurṭubī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān transmit star setting with the tree or vegetation's shadow. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds the descending star, ground-hugging plants, and trees bending in wind or lowering branches for fruit and leaves; he cites Imruʾ al-Qays's face-first leaning image for this figurative descent."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p5", "position": "Their form and activity disclose the Creator's workmanship and call for submission.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr says their form and power show workmanship requiring submission; al-Ṭabrisī says origination and artistry are visible in them, while their shadows also disclose a directing Creator. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes rational signs of divine making and subjection from symbolic or imaginative signs accessible to differing minds."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p6", "position": "They prostrate morning and evening.", "reasons": "Mujāhid gives this timing for trees, star and tree, or the stars together with trees, in the several transmissions."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p7", "position": "The stars can prostrate literally.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq permits literal celestial prostration and cites 16:12. Al-Zajjāj finds the celestial reading possible because 22:18 names the sun, moon and stars among prostrating beings."}, {"id": "55:6/q03/p8", "position": "Inwardly, souls or faculties turn toward their appointed end.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī's animal and vegetative souls turn to the body's earth for nurture; al-Ālūsī's lower powers and higher predispositions humble themselves upon return to God; Bursawī says reason and thought cannot encompass the Creator."}]}
{"id": "55:6/q04", "question": "Why is yasjudān dual?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:6/q04/p1", "position": "It agrees with the two named kinds, even though each noun is collective.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda says the two subjects are dual in wording; Ibn ʿAṭiyya illustrates collective nouns with dual verbs in poetry; al-Majāz likewise matches the two nouns. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kisāʾī observe that two nonhuman collectives often take one singular verb, although a dual is valid; al-Wāḥidī adds that the dual suits the line endings. Al-Kisāʾī heard both sūdān and sūd of two black sheep; al-Farrāʾ favored sūd. Al-Farrāʾ says masculine sheep with feminine camels usually take singular feminine but either-gender dual is valid; in 'your people and their camels came', a human plural may mean the handlers or both mixed groups."}]}

{"id": "55:6/q09", "question": "What do the verse's prostrating beings teach people?", "turns_on": "The notes draw ethical, theological and cosmic lessons from the same obedience.", "positions": [{"id": "55:6/q09/p1", "position": "They call people to obey and worship God gratefully.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says natural obedience should lead humans to willing prostration and gratitude; Kuran Yolu contrasts involuntary plant obedience with the dignity of conscious human reverence. {"id": "55:8/q04", "question": "What does ṭughyān or transgressing mean here?", "turns_on": "The sense of ṭughyān follows whether the balance is justice, a weighing device, or judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q04/p1", "position": "It is going beyond the proper limit of justice or right, thus committing injustice or oppression.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn al-Shaykh as cited by al-Būrsawī, and others gloss it as excess, inclination, oppression or exceeding fairness. The Study Quran's Aj cites 11:84 and 83:1–3 when explaining withholding dues."}, {"id": "55:8/q04/p3", "position": "With the balance as judgment, it is distorting a judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this conditional explanation; al-Qurṭubī repeats it alongside the justice and physical-scale senses."}]}
{"id": "55:8/q05", "question": "What does الميزان denote in this command?", "turns_on": "Whether balance names a material device or the action of weighing, justice or judgment, or the Qur'an and religious order; several authors intentionally combine senses.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q05/p1", "position": "It is a physical scale or measuring instrument used for quantities and fair transactions.", "reasons": "Muqātil connects the balance with measures. Al-Māwardī reports Muqātil's weighing-goods interpretation; al-Zamakhsharī extends it to every instrument for weighing or measuring quantities, used in transactions and giving and taking. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says the ordinary scale is most likely here because the following injunctions require fair weight. Al-Rāzī says the repeated noun supports weighing and includes exchanges and like-for-like sales."}, {"id": "55:8/q05/p2", "position": "It is justice or a standard of right, encompassing due order and equity.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports Mujāhid's justice reading; al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Zajjāj's. Al-Rāzī says 'setting the balance' can mean prescribing justice. Al-Biqāʿī extends justice to both cosmic realms; the Qur'an measures knowledge and a scale measures sensible things. Asad calls it a standard of right. Kuran Yolu describes divinely given religious and ethical order, with justice putting things in place, rejecting false divinity and giving rights-holders their due. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes both justice and devices together, and sees convergent word senses. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ permits the earlier balance to be any truth or justice standard."}, {"id": "55:8/q05/p3", "position": "It is weighing itself, with the instrument's noun standing for the act.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī prefers weighing or justice for this second occurrence, compares using 'trust' for trusting and 'appointed time' for promising, and says repetition and the surrounding phrase support weighing."}, {"id": "55:8/q05/p4", "position": "It is judgment, whose transgression is distortion.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī supplies this third conditional sense; al-Qurṭubī repeats it."}, {"id": "55:8/q05/p5", "position": "It can be the Qur'an as the foundation and measure of religion.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this alternative and says the Qur'an joins rational with transmitted evidence; al-Biqāʿī likewise calls the Qur'an a balance for knowledge beside the material scale."}]}
{"id": "55:8/q06", "question": "How broad is the conduct governed by the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the balance is applied to commercial measures alone or also to moral, religious and inward order; these scopes are compatible in sources that combine senses.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q06/p1", "position": "It governs fair dealings and giving other people their due in measures, weights, and transactions.", "reasons": "Qatāda urges doing for others what one wants from them, since justice sustains society; al-Būrsawī repeats this in measures. Ibn ʿAbbās warns of the ruin caused by measures and weights and corrects a man overweighing, citing 55:9. Al-Zamakhsharī applies instruments to judgments and transactions. Al-Rāzī says the wording includes both weighing for a customer and a seller's taking excess for himself in exchange or like-for-like sales. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says shortchanging can harm buyer or seller."}, {"id": "55:8/q06/p2", "position": "It also governs justice in worship, knowledge, action, spiritual states, rights, and the match between inner and outer life.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī includes rights owed to God and people, sincerity in deeds, truthfulness in states, and no deceit or hidden shirk inwardly. {"id": "55:8/q07", "question": "Does the prohibition cover unavoidable measurement error?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q07/p1", "position": "No; it targets deliberate excess, while humanly unavoidable imprecision is excused.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān make the same distinction between deliberate overstepping and inescapable error."}]}
{"id": "55:8/q08", "question": "Why repeat الميزان in this passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the repetition chiefly specifies the prohibition, emphasizes justice, or carries distinct and layered senses.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q08/p1", "position": "Repetition states explicitly the object whose transgression is prohibited.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives this explanation while reporting the Qur'an sense of balance."}, {"id": "55:8/q08/p2", "position": "Repetition underlines justice as fundamental to creation and human transactions.", "reasons": "The Study Quran explicitly connects three repetitions with this emphasis."}, {"id": "55:8/q08/p3", "position": "The repeated noun permits distinct or overlapping senses in its occurrences.", "reasons": "A view reported by al-Rāzī makes the first balance justice and the second the instrument; he prefers the reverse, the first instrument and the second weighing or justice. {"id": "55:8/q09", "question": "Why name the balance and say 'in the balance' here?", "turns_on": "The first explanation concerns the chosen noun and the second the scope conveyed by the preposition; the notes do not set them against each other.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q09/p1", "position": "Naming the instrument extends the ban to unfair weighing on either side of a transaction.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says 'in weighing' might be heard as only weighing for a customer, whereas the instrument noun also stops a seller taking excess for himself, especially in exchange and like-for-like sales."}, {"id": "55:8/q09/p2", "position": "The metaphorical 'in' bars even a slight transgression involving the balance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts such partial involvement with destroying the entire balance and cites 4:5 and a verse by Ṣabra for partial use of something."}]}

{"id": "55:8/q11", "question": "How does the surrounding passage develop this command?", "turns_on": "The notes trace different connections: creation and cosmic order, the next weighing command, or the audience established before the refrain.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q11/p1", "position": "The raised sky and created order lead into the balance and a human duty to maintain justice.", "reasons": "Muqātil places it after prostration of stemless plants and trees through moving shadows and the sky raised 500 years above earth. Al-Burhān describes the balance between the paired sky and earth in the sūra's paired structure, citing 55:3–7, 10, 14–15, 17 and 19. The Study Quran reports, without grading, the Prophet's saying that heavens and earth are founded on justice."}, {"id": "55:8/q11/p2", "position": "The following command to establish fair weight and prohibition of loss clarify or reinforce this prohibition.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj appeals to 55:9 in favor of a prohibitive construction; Ibn ʿAbbās cites 55:9 while correcting a man at the scale. {"id": "55:8/q12", "question": "What reported incidents or sayings illustrate this injunction?", "turns_on": "These are different reported warnings, actions, exhortations and sayings rather than competing versions of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q12/p1", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās warned the mawālī that failures in measures and weights ruined earlier peoples.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī transmits the warning; al-Māwardī repeats it while explaining short measure."}, {"id": "55:8/q12/p2", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās saw a man overweigh, told him to straighten the balance, and cited the next verse.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports the encounter and the citation of 55:9."}, {"id": "55:8/q12/p3", "position": "Qatāda urged reciprocal fairness in dealings and fulfilment of dues because justice sustains society.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports his counsel; al-Būrsawī repeats it with specific reference to fulfilling measures as one wishes others to do."}, {"id": "55:8/q12/p4", "position": "The Prophet is reported to have said that the heavens and earth are founded on justice.", "reasons": "The Study Quran gives this report without a grading."}]}
{"id": "55:8/q13", "question": "How should Qur'anic eloquence and alleged imitations be assessed?", "turns_on": "Whether transmitted-era Arabic eloquence tests Qur'anic expression or the Qur'an supplies the standard, and how much attention alleged imitations merit.", "positions": [{"id": "55:8/q13/p1", "position": "The Qur'an itself should be the sound standard for Arabic usage, and feeble imitations by later pretenders deserve little standing.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes al-Khaṭṭābī's test against eloquence transmitted in the compilation era. She still values his early rhetorical and critical discussion but says his attention to later prophetic pretenders' imitations gives them undeserved standing."}, {"id": "55:8/q13/p2", "position": "Qur'anic expressions can be defended against claims of departure from accepted eloquent Arabic by examining poetic conventions and alleged imitations.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Khaṭṭābī's method and his treatment of Musaylima's poor efforts; she objects to its standard and to giving such imitations attention, while valuing his critical discussion."}]}

{"id": "55:39/q02", "question": "What sequence does the initial fāʾ mark?", "turns_on": "Temporal succession, immediate consequence, or rhetorical order.", "positions": [{"id": "55:39/q02/p1", "position": "It marks temporal succession after the sky splits.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī lists this possibility."}, {"id": "55:39/q02/p2", "position": "It marks immediate consequence: punishment begins without time for questioning.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts undelayed afterlife punishment with worldly delay, citing 55:31."}, {"id": "55:39/q02/p3", "position": "It orders the warning: after escape through heaven is denied, offenders have no time even to answer.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this rhetorical sequence."}]}

{"id": "55:41/q04", "question": "Who are the criminals named here?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording refers generally to the condemned, to named opponents, or inwardly to people ruled by vices.", "positions": [{"id": "55:41/q04/p1", "position": "The guilty or unbelievers among humans and jinn.", "reasons": "Muqātil places recognition after judgment; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the immediate threat addresses the unbelieving majority of both kinds at revelation; al-Ālūsī says the explicit noun singles out sinners among humans and jinn."}, {"id": "55:41/q04/p2", "position": "Abū Jahl, al-Aswad, al-Walīd, and al-Naḍr.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī transmits this identification from ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "55:41/q04/p3", "position": "Those dominated by entrenched bodily vices.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says acquired dispositions and vices show outwardly."}]}

{"id": "55:41/q06", "question": "What does sīmāhum mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:41/q06/p1", "position": "Their identifying signs or distinguishing marks.", "reasons": "Majāz and al-Naḥḥās gloss sīmā as a mark; Ibn Qutayba gives black faces and blue eyes as examples; al-Bursawī notes sīmā and sīmiyāʾ with kasra, shortened or lengthened; al-Rāzī derives it from original sawmā, like ḍayzā in form; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ locates the conspicuous mark on the face."}]}
{"id": "55:41/q07", "question": "What signs identify the criminals?", "turns_on": "Which visible condition counts as the identifying sign.", "positions": [{"id": "55:41/q07/p1", "position": "Blackened faces and blue eyes.", "reasons": "Muqātil places these signs after judgment; al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Jurayj and many exegetes report them. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī cite 3:106 and 20:102; al-Zajjāj also connects 37:24; Ibn Kathīr contrasts believers' ablution radiance."}, {"id": "55:41/q07/p2", "position": "Other disfigurements, including blindness, muteness, deafness, and walking on their faces.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows other disfigurement; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī name blindness, muteness and deafness; al-Biqāʿī includes walking on faces with blue eyes and black faces."}, {"id": "55:41/q07/p3", "position": "Gloom, grief, dust, or sorrow visible on them.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī name gloom and sorrow or grief; al-Rāzī proposes dust and gloom; al-Ālūsī reports grief and gloom."}, {"id": "55:41/q07/p4", "position": "Brands on their foreheads.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī links this possibility to the branding of foreheads in 9:35."}, {"id": "55:41/q07/p5", "position": "The visible effects of acquired vices.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says entrenched bodily dispositions become outward signs."}, {"id": "55:41/q07/p6", "position": "Signs of disgrace.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this explanation without specifying a physical mark."}]}
